title: Charity is patient (1 Corinthians 13:1–7)
hookLine: charity is patient, is kind, envieth not

lines: NO: FOR A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.
cards: It's often read at weddings, so it's easy to assume it was written for one. It wasn't.
Paul was writing to a church that was quarreling: over which leader to follow, over food, over who had the most impressive spiritual gift. Right in the middle of his argument about gifts, he stops.
I'll show you, he says, a more excellent way. Then he writes the passage that has long outlived the quarrel.

teach.b: He begins by making every gift worthless without it: "If I speak with the tongues of men, and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."
Then he describes charity, and not as a feeling.

teach.h: NOT A FEELING: WHAT IT DOES.
teach.b: He lists what it does and what it won't do: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely; is not puffed up." It isn't ambitious, doesn't seek its own, isn't provoked to anger, thinks no evil.
Then four alls: "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things."
Why charity and not love? Paul's Greek word is agapē. Saint Jerome's Latin Bible rendered it caritas, and the Douay-Rheims followed the Latin.
So, here, did the King James. Newer English translations tend to say love. In everyday English, charity has shrunk to mean giving money.
In Catholic teaching it keeps the old, large meaning: the Catechism calls charity the virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God.
Some readers try a simple exercise: read the passage again with their own name where it says charity.
Patient, kind, not puffed up. The first line is the hard one. Of everything Paul could have put first, he put patience.

how: Catholics count charity as one of the three theological virtues with faith and hope, and 1 Corinthians 13 is one of the readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

o: self-giving love for God and neighbor
giving money to people in need
a group that raises funds for the poor

games.q: inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: 1 Corinthians 13 was written for a wedding
Paul wrote it to a church quarreling over gifts and leaders.
the King James Bible also says charity here
both it and the Douay-Rheims follow the old Latin caritas.
Paul defines charity mainly as a warm feeling
he lists what it does: patient, kind, not puffed up, bearing all things.

games.q: you're Paul, mid-argument with a church fighting over whose gift is greatest. what comes next in your letter?
o: rank the gifts from best to worst.
tell them gifts don't matter at all.
show them a more excellent way: charity.
games.why: he stops the argument and writes about charity: without it, even the tongues of angels are sounding brass.

practice: Think of the place you're most likely to lose patience today, a slow line, a child who won't put on shoes, a coworker who explains the same thing twice, and notice whatever starts to rise.
Then picture waiting it out one breath longer than usual, saying nothing sharp. If you pray, say charity is patient, is kind, slowly, as a prayer; if not, rest in that one longer breath.

wordCard.voice: Charity. The Douay-Rheims word for Paul's agapē: love that gives itself. The first thing he says it is: patient. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love. rendered caritas in Jerome's Latin, and charity in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Your line: one breath longer. And that's week eighty-two: reasonable service, moria, coadjutors, a temple, commemoration, one body, and charity. Day five hundred seventy-four.
